pl-l4d3c4-d1e115.summary: Asks whether baptism would be true if given in the name of the Father only, or of the Holy Spirit only, as it is when given in the name of Christ.

pl-l4d3c4-d1e118.summary: Reports that Ambrose seems to say that if the mystery of the Trinity is held by faith and only one person is named, the sacrament is full; and conversely, if three are named but one is wrongly thought of, the mystery is empty. Ambrose: if you deny one you overthrow all; naming one while not denying the others in faith gives a full sacrament, while naming three and diminishing the power of one empties it. In Christ's name the mystery is fulfilled by unity of name, and the Spirit is not separated from Christ's baptism.
claims: Naming one person with faith in the Trinity gives a full sacrament.
Naming three persons while denying one's power empties the sacrament.

pl-l4d3c4-d1e130.summary: Continues Ambrose: whether naming only the Spirit lacks nothing for the mystery's fullness. Reason shows that naming one signifies the Trinity: naming Christ designates the Father who anointed, the Son anointed, and the Spirit with whom he was anointed; naming the Father indicates his Son and Spirit if also grasped in the heart; naming the Spirit names the Father from whom he proceeds and the Son whose Spirit he is. Authority agrees: 'you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit'.
claims: Naming one divine person signifies the whole Trinity.
One can rightly be baptized in the Holy Spirit.

pl-l4d3c4-d1e137.summary: Concludes that true baptism is given in Christ's name, and that it seems true baptism can be given in the name of the Father only or of the Spirit only, if the baptizer holds the faith of the Trinity, understood in any of these names. But one who, believing perversely and intending to introduce error, names only one of the three does not fulfil the mystery.
claims: Baptism in one name is valid if the baptizer holds Trinitarian faith.
Naming one person to introduce error invalidates the baptism.

pl-l4d3c4-d1e140.summary: Interprets Ambrose's saying that the mystery is empty if the baptizer, naming all three, diminishes one person's power: this applies to one who neither intends nor believes himself to baptize, lacking not only faith but the intention of baptizing.
claims: The 'empty mystery' concerns one lacking the intention to baptize.

pl-l4d3c4-d1e146.summary: Concludes that one who baptizes in Christ's name baptizes in the Trinity's name, which is understood there. Still it is safer to name the three persons: 'in the name', not 'in the names', that is, in the invocation or confession of Father, Son, and Spirit, since the Trinity is invoked to work invisibly as the minister works visibly. Saying 'in the names' breaks the form, and there is no sacrament.
claims: It is safer to name all three persons.
'In the name', singular, is the required form.
Saying 'in the names' invalidates the sacrament.

pl-l4d3c4.summary: Asks whether baptism would be true in the name of the Father or the Spirit alone, as it is in the name of Christ. Ambrose seems to say that if the mystery of the Trinity is held by faith, naming one person gives a full sacrament, while naming all three while diminishing one person's power empties it; naming one person signifies the Trinity. Lombard concludes that baptism in Christ's name is true, and that baptism in the Father's or Spirit's name alone seems possible if the baptizer holds faith in the Trinity, but not if someone names one person to introduce error. Ambrose's 'empty mystery' concerns one who neither believes nor intends to baptize. It is safer to name the three persons, 'in the name', not 'in the names', which breaks the form.
claims: Baptism in the name of Christ is true baptism.
Baptism in the name of one person may be valid if the baptizer holds faith in the Trinity.
One who names one person to introduce error does not baptize.
It is safer to name all three persons.
Saying 'in the names' breaks the form.
